essays.stem: Compare an autocratic and a participative (democratic) leadership style, and recommend when a manager of a Kingston hotel should use each.
essays.modelAnswer: In an autocratic style, the leader decides alone and gives clear instructions that staff are expected to follow. It is fast and gives clear control, but it can make staff feel undervalued, wastes their knowledge and may lower motivation if used all the time. In a participative style, the leader involves staff in decisions, asks for ideas and often reaches a decision together with them. It makes better use of staff experience, raises commitment and helps people grow, but it takes longer and is not suitable when a decision must be made at once. A hotel manager should use an autocratic, directive approach in emergencies, such as a fire alarm or a guest falling ill, and where rules leave no choice, such as food safety or cash handling procedures. She should use a participative approach for decisions where staff know the work best and where their support matters, such as planning a new breakfast service, changing rosters or improving guest check-in. A good leader moves between styles to suit the situation and the people.
markingPoints: Describes the autocratic style with a strength and a weakness
Describes the participative style with a strength and a weakness
Recommends autocratic use for emergencies or fixed rules, with hotel examples
Recommends participative use where staff knowledge and support matter, with examples
Concludes that the style should suit the situation and people

essays.stem: Staff morale at a Montego Bay call centre is low, absence is high and many people leave within a year. Using at least one motivation theory, recommend what the operations manager should do.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first find out the causes through a short anonymous staff survey, exit interview records and talks with team leaders. Herzberg's theory is useful here. Hygiene factors such as fair pay, a clean and safe workplace, reliable equipment, fair rosters and decent break areas must be right, because if they are poor, staff will be unhappy whatever else is done. I would fix any of these problems that the survey shows, such as broken headsets or unfair shift swaps. But hygiene factors alone will not motivate. I would add motivators: regular recognition from team leaders for good calls, a clear path from agent to senior agent and team leader, chances to train in new types of calls, and more say in how targets are met. Maslow's ideas also apply: staff need security and belonging, so a good induction and a buddy for new starters would help. I would train team leaders to coach rather than only check statistics. I would track absence, turnover and survey scores each quarter to see whether the changes are working.
markingPoints: Finds the causes first through survey, exit data or talks
Applies a named theory correctly (for example Herzberg's hygiene factors and motivators)
Recommends fixing hygiene or basic needs where they are poor
Recommends motivators such as recognition, career path, training or more say
Includes team leader development and measures to track progress

essays.stem: Explain the stages of Tuckman's model of team development, and describe what a leader should do at each stage for a newly formed project team.
essays.modelAnswer: In the forming stage, members are polite and unsure, and they look to the leader for direction. The leader should explain the team's purpose and goals, help members get to know each other and set out roles and basic ground rules. In the storming stage, members start to challenge each other, the leader and the methods, and conflict appears. The leader should not panic or hide it, but listen, clarify roles, deal openly with disagreements and keep the focus on the goal. In the norming stage, the team agrees how it will work, trust grows and members cooperate. The leader can step back a little, encourage members to take on more responsibility and support the team's own rules. In the performing stage, the team works well with little direction and solves its own problems. The leader should delegate, provide resources, remove obstacles and develop individuals. Many writers add a fifth stage, adjourning, when the project ends. The leader should recognise the team's achievement, capture lessons learned and help members move on.
markingPoints: Explains forming and the leader's role (purpose, roles, ground rules)
Explains storming and the leader's role (handle conflict, clarify roles)
Explains norming and the leader's role (step back, encourage responsibility)
Explains performing and the leader's role (delegate, resource, develop)
Mentions adjourning, with recognition and lessons learned

essays.stem: A busy operations manager at a Portmore distribution firm wants to delegate more of her work. Describe the steps she should follow to delegate effectively, and explain the benefits.
essays.modelAnswer: First she should list her tasks and decide which can be delegated, keeping those that need her authority, such as discipline, confidential pay matters or the budget. Then she should choose the right person for each task, matching skills, interest and current workload, and seeing it as a chance to develop staff. She should explain the task clearly: the result wanted, why it matters, the deadline, the standard and any limits. She must give the person enough authority and resources, and tell others who need to know that the person is now in charge of the task. She should agree check-in points rather than watching every step, and be available for questions. When the task is done, she should review it with the person, give feedback and recognise good work. She remains accountable for the outcome. The benefits are that she frees time for planning and leadership, staff gain skills and confidence, decisions are made closer to the work, and the firm builds people who could step up in future.
markingPoints: Decides which tasks can and cannot be delegated
Chooses the right person by skill, workload and development
Explains the result, standard, deadline and authority, and informs others
Agrees check-in points, supports, and reviews with feedback, staying accountable
Explains benefits for the manager, staff and the firm

essays.stem: Two senior members of a marketing team in New Kingston no longer speak to each other after a dispute over credit for a campaign. Describe how you would resolve the conflict and rebuild the team.
essays.modelAnswer: I would act quickly, because the conflict affects the whole team's work. First I would meet each person privately to hear their side, listen without taking sides and find out the facts and feelings involved. I would then bring them together in a private, calm meeting with ground rules: speak in turn, focus on the issue, no personal attacks. I would ask each to explain their view and what they need, and help them see the other's point. Often the real issue is feeling undervalued, so I would acknowledge both people's contributions to the campaign. Together we would agree practical steps: for example, how credit will be shared in future, how work will be divided, and how they will raise problems early. I would record the agreement and check in with both after a week and a month. I would also look at the team's processes, such as making contributions visible in reports, so the same dispute does not happen again. If the conflict continued or became harassment, I would seek human resource advice and follow the firm's procedure.
markingPoints: Acts promptly and meets each person privately to hear both sides
Holds a joint meeting with ground rules, focused on issues not personalities
Acknowledges contributions and helps each understand the other
Agrees practical steps, records them and follows up
Fixes the underlying process and uses HR procedure if needed

essays.stem: Plan how a manager of a supermarket branch in May Pen should develop her team of 20 staff over the next year.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start with a training needs analysis. I would compare the skills the branch needs, such as customer service, stock control, the new point-of-sale system, food safety and supervision, with the skills each person has, using observation, records and a talk with each staff member about their own goals. From this I would write a simple development plan for the branch and a short plan for each person. I would use a mix of methods, because people learn in different ways: on-the-job coaching by experienced staff, job rotation between the tills, stockroom and deli, short courses for food safety and first aid, and online modules for the new system. For two or three staff with potential, I would plan supervisory development, such as acting as shift leader, as part of succession planning. I would set aside a budget and protected time for training, so it is not dropped when the store is busy. Each quarter I would review progress with each person, and at the end of the year I would check the effect on results such as errors, customer complaints and staff turnover.
markingPoints: Carries out a training needs analysis comparing needed and current skills
Writes branch and individual development plans that include staff goals
Uses a mix of methods (coaching, rotation, courses, online learning)
Includes succession planning for staff with potential
Sets budget and time and evaluates the effect on results

essays.stem: Explain why a manager should care about the wellbeing of the people she leads, and describe practical steps she can take in a busy workplace.
essays.modelAnswer: Staff wellbeing matters for people and for the business. Staff who are overworked, stressed or unwell make more mistakes, are absent more often and are more likely to leave, which raises costs and harms service. A manager also has a legal and ethical duty to provide a safe and healthy workplace, and this includes the risks from stress and long hours as well as physical hazards. When staff feel cared for, they are more committed and loyal. In a busy workplace, the manager can plan workloads realistically, set clear priorities and share work fairly, so a few people are not overloaded. She should make sure staff take their breaks and leave, and plan cover for peak times. She can hold regular one-to-ones where staff can raise concerns, and watch for signs such as more errors, absence or irritability. She should know where to refer staff for support, such as an employee assistance service, and keep any personal matters confidential. She should also set an example by not sending messages late at night and by taking her own breaks.
markingPoints: Explains the effects of poor wellbeing on errors, absence and turnover
Explains the legal and ethical duty for a safe and healthy workplace
Describes realistic workload planning and fair sharing of work
Describes breaks, leave, one-to-ones and watching for signs of stress
Describes referral to support, confidentiality and leading by example

essays.stem: A garment factory in Kingston is moving its sewing team from individual piecework to small team cells. As team manager, plan how you would lead your staff through this change.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by making sure I understand the change myself: why the firm is making it, how it will work, and what it means for pay, roles and targets. I would then explain it to the team in person, early and honestly, including the reasons, such as faster orders and fewer defects, and what will stay the same. I would expect worry, especially about pay, and give people time to ask questions. I would meet staff in small groups and one-to-one to hear their concerns, and pass these to senior managers. Where possible I would involve staff in the design, for example in choosing cell members or arranging machines. I would identify respected staff who support the change and ask them to help others. Training in new skills and team working would be given before the change starts, and we might pilot one cell first. During the change I would keep people informed, check progress daily, solve problems quickly and celebrate early successes. Afterwards I would review results and staff views, and adjust the system where needed.
markingPoints: Understands the reasons and effects of the change before briefing staff
Communicates early and honestly, and listens to concerns
Involves staff in designing the change and uses supportive colleagues
Provides training and pilots before full roll-out
Keeps informing, solves problems, celebrates progress and reviews afterwards

essays.stem: Discuss how a manager can make sure that all members of a mixed team are treated fairly, and why this matters.
essays.modelAnswer: A fair manager treats everyone with respect and makes decisions on clear, job-related grounds. To do this she should apply the same rules, standards and procedures to everyone, whether for rosters, overtime, leave, training or discipline. Decisions should be based on evidence, such as skills and results, not on friendship, gender, age, religion, disability or background. She should explain the reasons for decisions so staff can see they are fair. Opportunities such as training, acting roles and interesting projects should be shared, not always given to the same people. She should make reasonable changes so that staff with a disability or caring duties can take part fully. She must also deal quickly with any bullying, harassment or unfair comments, and give everyone a safe way to raise concerns. Fair treatment matters because it builds trust and morale, reduces conflict and staff turnover, and helps the firm use the talents of all its people. Unfair treatment can also break employment law and the firm's policies, leading to grievances and damage to the firm's name.
markingPoints: Applies the same rules and standards to all, based on job-related evidence
Explains decisions and shares opportunities fairly
Makes reasonable changes for staff with disabilities or caring duties
Deals with bullying or harassment and offers a safe way to raise concerns
Explains why it matters: trust, morale, retention, law and reputation

essays.stem: A new branch manager at a Mandeville credit union must turn a group of staff into a team with a shared goal. Describe how she should set direction and build commitment in her first three months.
essays.modelAnswer: In her first weeks she should listen and learn: meet each staff member, ask about their work, what works well and what frustrates them, and study the branch's results and member feedback. This shows respect and gives her the facts. She should then share the credit union's goals and explain what they mean for the branch, for example growing loans to small farmers while keeping arrears low. With the team, she should agree a few clear branch goals and measures, such as loan turnaround time and member satisfaction, so staff feel ownership. Each person should know their part in reaching them. She should hold short weekly team meetings to review progress, share information and solve problems together. Early on she should deliver some quick wins, such as fixing a problem staff raised, to build trust. She should recognise good work, treat everyone fairly and lead by example in punctuality, service and integrity. By the end of three months she should review progress with the team and adjust the plan.
markingPoints: Starts by listening to staff and studying results
Explains the organisation's goals and links them to the branch
Agrees clear branch goals, measures and individual roles with the team
Builds commitment through regular meetings, quick wins and recognition
Leads by example and reviews progress after three months

practical1.title: Plan the set-up of a new team: charter, roles and delegation plan
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a case: a made-up Jamaican firm is creating a new team of eight staff (for example a customer care team for a new branch of a hardware chain in Old Harbour) and has given you a list of tasks, the staff members' skills and the team's goals. As the management group, plan how the team will be set up and led. Give each member a named role: lead manager (chairs the group and writes the team purpose and goals), roles planner (matches staff to roles using their skills and draws the team structure chart), delegation planner (writes a delegation plan: which tasks go to whom, with authority, deadlines and check-in points), development planner (lists training needs and a 3-month development plan), and team charter writer (drafts the team's ground rules, communication routine and how conflict will be handled). In a group of four, the lead manager also writes the charter. Bring the parts together on flipchart sheets and in one short document, then present it to the assessor in 10 minutes. Every member presents their part.
materials: Case brief and staff skills list from the assessor
Computers with word processor and spreadsheet software
Flipchart paper, sticky notes and markers
photos: The team purpose and goals on flipchart
The team structure chart with roles matched to skills
The delegation plan with authority, deadlines and check-in points
The training needs list and development plan
The team charter and the group presenting
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the plan
Team goals are clear, specific and linked to the case
Roles are matched to the skills given, with a fair spread of work
Delegation plan states the result, authority, deadline and check-in points for each task
Development plan targets real gaps and uses suitable methods
Charter includes ground rules, communication routine and a way to handle conflict
Presented their part clearly and answered questions
safety: Use only the made-up staff details in the case; do not discuss real colleagues
Keep all papers with the group and hand them to the assessor at the end
Respect each other's views; challenge ideas, not people
Share the workload fairly and take a short break

practical2.title: Lead a team meeting through a change and a one-to-one coaching talk
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a case: a made-up Jamaican workplace (for example the housekeeping team of a Runaway Bay hotel) must change its shift pattern next month, and one experienced staff member is unhappy about it. The group runs two role plays. In the first, a 20-minute team meeting, the team leader explains the change, listens to concerns and agrees next steps with the team. In the second, a 10-minute one-to-one, the team leader talks privately with the unhappy staff member and agrees how to support them. Give each member a named role: team leader (plans and leads both meetings using a written plan), unhappy staff member (plays the role card from the assessor), team members (one or two members play staff with the views on their role cards), and note-taker and observer (records the concerns raised and actions agreed, and scores the leader on an observer checklist). Swap roles for a short second run of the one-to-one so that at least two members practise the team leader role. Afterwards the group writes a one-page summary for staff confirming the change, the reasons and the support agreed.
materials: Case brief and role cards from the assessor
Meeting plan, observer checklist and action log templates
Computer with word processor software and printer
Table and chairs set up as a meeting room
photos: The team leader's written plan for both meetings
The team meeting in progress, showing the set-up and flipchart (faces only if all agree)
The flipchart list of concerns raised and actions agreed
The observer's completed checklists for each team leader
The one-page staff summary of the change and support
checklist: Prepared a clear plan for the meetings based on the case
Explained the change and the reasons in plain, honest terms
Listened to concerns without becoming defensive and checked understanding
Agreed practical next steps and support with owners and dates
Handled the unhappy staff member privately, respectfully and fairly
